units.content: Connecting to Compete 2025 introduces the Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0), a fundamental redesign of the World Bank’s former survey-based Logistics Performance Index toward a system grounded in shipment-level data. Drawing on large-scale tracking data from maritime, aviation, and postal operators—together accounting for over 80 percent of global goods trade—the LPI 2.0 provide standardized and comparable measures of supply chain connectivity, speed, and reliability across economies and over time. The framework comprises 21 indicators, including 6 core indicators capturing direct connectivity and import time performance in each mode and 15 supplementary indicators that shed light on maritime competition, transshipment dependence, corridor performance for landlocked developing countries, and postal logistics for e-commerce. Data for 2023–24 reveal large variations in connectivity across regions, substantial time penalties associated with transshipment and border procedures, and high unpredictability concentrated at ports, transshipment hubs, and inland checkpoints—particularly for imports and for landlocked countries. By shifting the focus from perceptions to observed outcomes, the LPI 2.0 significantly enhance diagnostic precision and policy relevance, enabling governments to better prioritize reforms with the highest potential impact on supply chain connectivity, speed, reliability, and resilience.
units.section: About this report

units.content: Logistics underpins the movement of goods and the operation of supply chains within and across borders. Efficient logistics reduces trade costs, connects firms to markets, and supports development, greatly increasing the volume and value of trade. Recent disruptions have underscored that resilient, well-functioning global logistics networks are essential for growth and welfare. They help countries withstand shocks, such as natural disasters, conflict, and technical failures, by ensuring reliable access to strategic goods that are too costly or impossible to produce domestically.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: The Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0) represent a major methodological shift toward shipment-level, real-world evidence. Drawing on large volumes of tracking data from maritime, aviation, and postal operators—modes that jointly account for more than 80 percent of the global goods trade—the LPI 2.0 provide standardized indicators of logistics performance across economies and time. Unlike the original Logistics Performance Index (LPI), which was based on surveys of logistics professionals, the LPI 2.0 measure the speed, reliability, and connectivity of supply chains based on observed shipment data. Note: Connecting to Compete 2023 featured a hybrid approach, presenting results from both the original LPI survey of logistics professionals and from supply chain tracking data. In 2025 the LPI 2.0 began using supply chain tracking data exclusively.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: The LPI 2.0’s 21 indicators provide deep insight into the functioning of logistics networks. Six core indicators (one connectivity indicator and one time indicator for maritime, air, and postal logistics) and 15 supplementary (connectivity and time) indicators provide insights into maritime competition, transshipment burdens, corridor performance for landlocked developing countries (LLDCs), and postal logistics for e-commerce. Core connectivity indicators capture the number of countries that can be reached directly via maritime, air cargo, or postal services, while core time indicators measure import dwell times and delivery times—key proxies for logistics efficiency and reliability.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: The shift to LPI 2.0 expands coverage, enhances comparability, and deepens diagnostic power, enabling policymakers to identify binding constraints with far greater precision. Data on all 21 indicators are published for 2023 and 2024 at https://lpi.worldbank.org, with options for comparisons across economies and over time.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Five main findings stand out from the analysis of the LPI 2.0:
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: There are large connectivity gaps across and within regions. On average, the Europe and Central Asia region and the North America region tend to exhibit the strongest connectivity, depending on the logistics mode, while Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean lag behind. These patterns reflect income, geography, and market accessibility. Within regions, some developing economies, such as Malaysia, Morocco, and Sri Lanka, showcase stronger performance due to their emergence as regional hubs.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Direct connections matter. Roughly half of containers worldwide require at least one transshipment. Each transshipment adds about 18 days to maritime lead times, creating structural disadvantages for small, remote economies.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Several low- and middle-income economies clear imported containers within a few days, which is comparable to high-income economies, while others experience import dwell times exceeding 10 days. Longer dwell times are due to weak customs automation, inefficient risk management, and cumbersome inspection and clearance processes. Aviation dwell times are shorter than those for containers because air cargo typically involves smaller volumes, higher value goods, and more integrated logistics systems.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: LLDCs face some of the longest and most unpredictable import times globally, with most delays stemming from idling at ports, border controls, and inland checkpoints. LLDCs must transit coastal countries, often crossing multiple borders and facing complex transit procedures. Corridor lead times and dwell times at the port of arrival dominate total import time, underscoring the importance of regional coordination, interoperable transit guarantees, and streamlined border procedures to improve reliability.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Delays are most unpredictable when goods are stationary—in ports and transshipment facilities—and more so for imports than exports. Aviation supply chains show especially high dispersion. Unpredictability imposes heavy costs on firms: it disrupts production planning, increases inventory needs, and reduces competitiveness in just-in-time and perishable goods markets. Digital visibility systems, such as those implemented in India and the United States, demonstrate how the value of real-time tracking can mitigate these risks.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Although logistics services are provided mainly by private operators, public policy is fundamental to the performance of global supply and value chains. The LPI 2.0 enable governments to prioritize interventions with the highest potential impact on supply chain speed, reliability, and resilience, tailored to country circumstances. Policy interventions should be implemented in a targeted, coherent manner across three strategic areas:
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Enhancing connectivity. Open transport and logistics markets to competition, invest in multimodal corridors and logistics clusters, and use regional integration and shared connectivity solutions so smaller or remote economies can benefit from economies of scale.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Reducing time and variability. Modernize border management through digitalization and risk-based controls (trade facilitation), improve port and airport performance, and strengthen traceability to make supply chains faster and more predictable.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Strengthening institutions and regulation. Build a robust governance framework with transparent public–private partnerships, competitive logistics markets, and coordinated policies across ministries, departments, and agencies to sustain and scale logistics reforms.
units.section: Executive summary

units.content: Logistics consists of a set of activities (freight transportation, warehousing, brokerage) that move goods and establish supply chains across and within borders. Logistics performance captures the efficiency of supply chain connections, measured in time, cost, and reliability. Since 2007 the Logistics Performance Index (LPI) initiative has emphasized the importance of efficient supply chains in connecting firms to markets, reducing trade costs, and supporting development. Logistics performance supports economic development by enabling trade within and across borders.

units.subsection: Why is logistics important for trade and development?
subsection_path: Why is logistics important for trade and development?

units.content: Economics literature, often using the survey-based LPI, has established that logistics performance positively and significantly impacts the volume and value of bilateral trade, in particular exports. Logistics influences the time required for a product to reach its market. On average, an increase in inland transit time of one day reduces exports by 7 percent. For manufactured goods exports the likelihood of a country exporting to the United States decreases by 1.5 percent for each additional day of shipping time. Note: Hummels 2001. Manufactures exports refers to goods in categories 7 (machinery) and 8 (miscellaneous manufactures) of the Standard International Trade Classification. For all types of goods (not just manufactures), the decrease in likelihood is 1 percent.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0

subsection_path: Why is logistics important for trade and development?

units.content: Logistics inefficiencies hamper economies’ competitiveness because logistics affect manufacturing firms’ production costs. Improved logistics performance reduces production costs and is linked to stronger participation in global value chains. This is achieved not just through lower direct logistics costs (transport, storage, and administrative costs) but also by reducing the need for inventory and working capital.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0
units.subsection: Why is logistics important for trade and development?
subsection_path: Why is logistics important for trade and development?

units.content: A series of disruptions of global logistics networks in recent years has underlined how well-functioning logistics networks are essential to production and welfare worldwide. Resilient logistics networks strengthen economies’ capacity to withstand natural disasters, conflict, technical failures, or other shocks by securing reliable access to strategic goods (such as pharmaceuticals, food, energy, and technologies) that are prohibitively costly to produce domestically or cannot be produced at all. Note: The World Bank’s Global Supply Chain Stress Index measures the magnitude of container shipping disruptions affecting global supply chains.

units.content: Cost is not directly measured by the LPI 2.0; however, two connectivity indicators highlight competition within the maritime sector, higher degrees of which tend to be associated with lower logistics costs.

units.content: Connectivity is positively associated with logistics performance across all modes. More connected economies can directly reach a larger number of trade partners and tend to face lower trade costs. Higher connectivity increases competition among logistics service providers and encourages investment in trade-related infrastructure, such as ports and information technology systems. It is also associated with a stronger presence of global logistics operators, which facilitates the diffusion of best practices and can generate positive spillovers for domestic logistics services. Connectivity is also critical for resilience. Economies that rely on only one or a few international partners are more vulnerable to disruptions when those links break down, whether due to natural disasters, conflict, technical failures, or other shocks.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0
units.subsection: Core indicators
subsection_path: Core indicators

units.content: The core time indicators measure the time it takes to import cargo. The core maritime and aviation time indicators are container import dwell time and aviation import dwell time, respectively. The core postal time indicator is the business-to-business delivery time, which captures customs clearance time and the time until the first attempted or final delivery. Import dwell and delivery times were selected as core indicators because customs procedures are generally more complex and time-consuming for imports than for exports, except in economies with strict export controls. In addition, for air cargo and postal shipments, event tracking is typically more complete and consistent for imports than for exports.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0
units.subsection: Core indicators
subsection_path: Core indicators

units.content: Three other maritime indicators gauge how economies could be affected by their dependence on third-country shipping hubs. These indicators are maritime lead time to import from port of arrival to the destination economy, time spent in transshipment, and number of transshipments for import containers. Two indicators that are derived from empty container movements—export supply chain initiation and import supply chain termination—reflect logistics efficiency among shippers, consignees, and trucking companies.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0
units.subsection: Supplementary indicators
subsection_path: Supplementary indicators

units.content: Two supplementary maritime time indicators capture additional aspects of performance at ports. Turnaround time (twenty-foot equivalent unit weighted and unweighted) reflects investment in port capacity and handling equipment, as well as the performance of terminal operations. Formalities such as obtaining certificates of origin, which are processed upstream, are not automated in many economies and may delay containers.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0
units.subsection: Supplementary indicators
subsection_path: Supplementary indicators

units.content: Since the launch of the LPI in 2007, the rapid digitization of global supply chains has transformed the availability and granularity of logistics data. The 2025 LPI 2.0 leverage this shift by moving beyond perception-based surveys and drawing on large-scale shipment-level tracking data obtained under information-sharing agreements with global operators. The World Bank collaborated with international carriers and data providers to assemble a multimodal dataset covering maritime shipping, air cargo, and postal services. This approach enables more objective, timely, and comparable indicators across economies.

units.content: The LPI 2.0 expand coverage relative to earlier editions, including many LLDCs and small island states that were previously excluded due to data gaps. Coverage remains limited for a small number of economies affected by embargoes or severe conflict, where global logistics operators have little or no presence. The dataset reflects actual logistics performance along international supply chains rather than national averages inferred from surveys.

Data

units.content: Maritime indicators draw on several complementary sources. Container shipping connectivity is derived from MDS Transmodal’s Containership Databank, which tracks container vessels and provides detailed information on service frequency and port rotations. Container dwell times, lead times, and supply chain initiation and termination indicators are calculated using shipment-level data from a major global shipping line. Port turnaround times are based on Automatic Identification System data from MarineTraffic, which records timestamped vessel arrivals and departures within geofenced port areas, enriched with ship and port registry information.
units.section: Chapter 1: Introducing the 2025 LPI 2.0
units.subsection: Supplementary indicators > Data
subsection_path: Supplementary indicators
Data

units.content: Aviation and postal indicators complement the maritime data by capturing time and connectivity in high-value and small-parcel trade. Air cargo indicators are based on data from Cargo iQ, an International Air Transport Association interest group, covering airport-to-airport shipments across more than 180 economies. Postal indicators rely on electronic tracking records from the Universal Postal Union, covering billions of international postal items annually and providing end-to-end timestamps from posting to final delivery.

units.content: Together, these datasets form the empirical backbone of the LPI 2.0, enabling a more granular and evidence-based assessment of logistics performance across economies and modes.

units.content: This chapter presents high-level findings from the Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0) with a focus on systematic patterns across regions and income groups. Data on all 21 indicators for 2023 and 2024 are published at https://lpi.worldbank.org, with options for comparisons across economies and over time.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance

units.content: On average, the Europe and Central Asia region and the North America region tend to have the highest connectivity across logistics modes, while the Latin America and the Caribbean region and the Sub-Saharan Africa region tend to have the lowest, depending on the mode considered (figure 2.1, panels a, b, c), although some developing economies perform strongly. This pattern mirrors broader income and geographic differences: high-income economies are generally more connected than low- and middle-income economies (figure 2.1, panels d, e, f). The connectivity indicators also reflect an economy’s position in the global shipping network and its proximity to centers of economic activity.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Connectivity
subsection_path: Connectivity

units.content: Developing economies that have emerged as regional or global shipping hubs, such as Malaysia, Morocco, and Sri Lanka, have much higher connectivity than their neighbors with the same accessibility. For the same level of market accessibility, larger economies have more connections—for instance, Australia and New Zealand, which are among the economies with the lowest accessibility, have the highest connectivity at that level of accessibility (figure 2.2).
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Connectivity
subsection_path: Connectivity

units.content: Connectivity increased during 2023–24 across most regions. Between 2023 and 2024 the number of direct liner shipping, aviation, and postal services connections increased across most income groups and regions, though some economies in South Asia and in the Middle East and North Africa showed a small decline (see figure 2.1). These declines in maritime connectivity occurred largely because of the Red Sea crisis.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Connectivity
subsection_path: Connectivity

units.content: The existence of direct maritime connections matters because it removes significant delays associated with transshipments. Though about half of containers travel directly to their destination, the rest may be transshipped multiple times—up to eight in some cases (figure 2.3, panel a). Small island states are the most affected, with several averaging more than two transshipments in 2024: São Tomé and Príncipe (2.6), Anguilla (2.4), the Comoros (2.4), and St. Kitts and Nevis (2.2). Each transshipment adds to maritime lead times—roughly 18 extra days per transfer—underscoring the heavy burden of hub dependence for these economies (figure 2.3, panel b). But the hub and spoke structure of modern long-distance supply chains, where smaller freight loads are consolidated into larger ones at hubs using high-capacity equipment, has proven cost-effective for carriers while providing small and peripheral economies with access to global routes.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Connectivity
subsection_path: Connectivity

units.content: Several low- and middle-income economies have moderate container import dwell times, similar to those in high-income economies, but many have exceptionally long ones (more than two weeks). Most of the economies with excessive dwell time are in Sub-Saharan Africa and in the Middle East and North Africa. Aviation import dwell time is typically only half of container import dwell time or less (figure 2.4). This difference reflects the smaller volume, smaller size, and higher value of air cargo compared with maritime cargo. Air cargo operations are more tightly integrated with door-to-door logistics chains, and a share of shipments is cleared by customs before arrival, whereas maritime cargo is usually cleared after arrival. Underperforming economies overlap between the two indicators. The economies with the shortest dwell times are typically active air cargo hubs, such as Belgium, the Netherlands, and Singapore.

units.subsection: Connectivity
subsection_path: Connectivity

units.content: Long container import dwell times often reflect inefficient processes for clearing imported goods. Poor performance may stem from limited automation in customs clearance and port logistics—areas that port community systems can help improve. Inadequate risk management and inefficient inspection practices by customs officials can also lengthen dwell times. Other requirements, including foreign exchange controls and inspections by agencies beyond customs, may further add to delays. Importer behavior can also contribute—for example, when importers use ports for storage. Note: Ollivier, Sahu, and Saragiotis 2024. Port community systems are electronic platforms that connect the systems operated by the many organizations that constitute a seaport, airport, or inland port community (European Port Community Systems Association, n.d.).

units.content: Business-to-business (B2B) postal delivery time is highly dispersed across low- and lower-middle-income economies. While this pattern is common to other logistics modes, underperforming economies differ somewhat across modes. The economies with the longest container and aviation import dwell times are concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa, whereas long B2B postal delivery times are more common in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Sub-Saharan Africa.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Time
subsection_path: Time

units.content: The differences between postal logistics performance and that of maritime containers and air cargo partly reflect the distinct facilities and processes involved in handling these different types of shipments. Two factors are especially important. First, geography and domestic distribution matter: The postal indicator includes both the time spent at the postal bureau of entry and the time until delivery, which can be prolonged when domestic postal networks are not optimized, particularly in geographically large economies. Second, customs clearance practices play a key role. In some economies, including several in Latin America and the Caribbean, inbound shipment information is not electronically linked to customs systems, so clearance relies on paper documentation for each shipment, increasing delays.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Time
subsection_path: Time

units.content: Landlocked developing countries (LLDCs) are among the most logistically constrained countries because their cargo needs to transit through coastal countries, crossing more than one border. As a result, the time to import a container is exceptionally long and uneven for LLDCs. Among the three components of time to import for LLDCs, corridor lead time and dwell time at port of arrival in coastal country tend to be the largest, followed by dwell time at destination (figure 2.5). In addition, dwell time at the port of arrival is longer for goods in transit than for goods destined for coastal countries.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: The special situation of landlocked developing countries
subsection_path: The special situation of landlocked developing countries

units.content: The long import times are not explained by corridor distance but by the considerable time cargo spends idling at ports, at borders, and in checkpoints along transit corridors en route to the LLDCs—reinforcing the importance of pursuing corridor reforms. These reforms include tackling border crossing delays, improving exchange of information on transit vehicles and goods across borders, and adopting better transit procedures and guarantee mechanisms. Among the biggest technical challenges is cross-border interoperability of financial guarantees or bonds covering the customs value of goods in transit. The best practice systems are the Transports Internationaux Routiers system (managed by the International Road Union and used in Central Asia and the Balkans) and the Common Transit procedure (applicable to European Union and European Free Trade Association countries). Except for the Secretary of Economic Integration of Central America transit system, these systems have not been fully adopted by other regions.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: The special situation of landlocked developing countries
subsection_path: The special situation of landlocked developing countries

units.content: The highest dispersion of dwell, delivery, and lead times occurs when goods are not in motion: in ports, border controls, and inland checkpoints. The LPI 2.0 assess supply chain reliability at the economy level through the interquartile range of dwell, delivery, and lead times (figure 2.6). Dispersion increases with median dwell times and is, on average, 36 percent higher for imports than for exports (figure 2.7). Dispersion is even higher for aviation supply chains. Note: The interquartile range measures the spread of the middle 50 percent of the distribution of delays. It is less sensitive to outliers than the standard deviation. Estimates of dispersion by economy and by indicator are available at https://lpi.worldbank.org/.

units.subsection: Assessing supply chain reliability using the dispersion of delays
subsection_path: Assessing supply chain reliability using the dispersion of delays

units.content: In well-functioning ports with seamless clearance systems, processing an unloaded container starts immediately. In Le Havre (France) 10 percent of containers leave the port in 1 day or less, 50 percent do so in 3.8 days or less, and only 25 percent take more than 5.9 days (figure 2.8). By contrast, in many ports only a few containers are cleared during the first few days after arrival. In Apapa (Nigeria) only 0.2 percent of containers leave the port in 1 day or less, 50 percent do so in 13.4 days or less, and 25 percent take more than 22.1 days, and in Algiers (Algeria), only 0.1 percent leave the port in 1 day or less, 50 percent do so in 17.6 days, and 25 percent take more than 26.3 days.
units.section: Chapter 2: What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
units.subsection: Assessing supply chain reliability using the dispersion of delays
subsection_path: Assessing supply chain reliability using the dispersion of delays

units.content: Dispersion reflects the unpredictability of port clearance processes and port operations, with adverse implications for supply and value chains. Unreliable control processes, especially for clearing imported goods, are associated with the complexity of the processes, which often require collecting paper documentation and complying with complicated foreign exchange regulations. With export dwell time, factors include operational constraints, such as slot availability, service frequency, and, in some economies, export clearances. Variations in shipper productivity and behavior can also affect the dispersion of export and import dwell time. The cost of unreliability can be substantial for firms’ inventories and operational planning, especially in just-in-time supply chains and those handling perishable goods.

units.content: Tracking goods with information technology platforms, known as supply chain visibility, helps firms hedge some of the consequences of unreliability. Technology can help firms better anticipate the next steps in the supply chain. Examples of recent large-scale visibility system include the Freight Logistics Optimization Works (FLOW) initiative in the United States and the Unified Logistics Information Platform in India. Note: See https://www.transportation.gov/freight-infrastructure-and-policy/flow for details on the FLOW initiative. India’s Unified Logistics Information Platform, launched in 2022 under the National E-Governance Plan, is a portal to make supply chain data generated by freight operators and government agencies accessible. It covers all logistics modes and encourages independent developers to propose visibility solutions for end users. The private sector has proposed more than 100 apps so far, highlighting the innovation potential of supply chain data.

units.content: In some low- and middle-income economies container ships spend an excessive time at port (figure 2.9, panel a). Port turnaround time reflects port handling capacity and productivity and is more directly shaped by infrastructure capacity and terminal management practices than by trade facilitation measures. In most upper-middle- and high-income economies the average weighted turnaround time is less than two days, compared with two to six days in several low- and lower-middle-income economies. These differences point to substantial scope for improving container port performance in low- and lower-middle-income economies.

units.content: For most countries, however, the most painful frictions are in trade facilitation and land-side logistics. This is evidenced by ship turnaround time typically being much shorter than container import dwell time (figure 2.9, panel b). Though dwell time is influenced by infrastructure, it captures primarily the performance of customs and other border procedures and therefore depends largely on trade facilitation policies.

units.content: Strong B2B and business-to-consumer (B2C) postal logistics performance is critical for e-commerce and SME participation. Although standard postal services experienced considerable market erosion in 2023 and 2024, they continue to play a substantial role in the last-mile delivery of cross-border e-commerce shipments (B2C), with close to 40 percent of these items being delivered by traditional postal services in 2024. Poor postal logistics performance tends to constrain small and medium enterprises (SMEs) from participating in e-commerce, with B2C SMEs usually finding it harder to scale up than B2B SMEs because B2C business entails a higher intensity of shipping. Furthermore, B2C postal delivery times tend to be longer than B2B delivery times, primarily in lower-middle-income economies, pointing to inconsistencies in postal logistics that penalize firms engaged in B2C e-commerce in these economies (figure 2.10).

units.content: Logistics services—such as freight transportation, warehousing, and brokerage—are delivered primarily by private firms. But their efficiency and the overall performance of supply chains are fundamentally shaped by public policy. Logistics operations depend on publicly funded infrastructure, must comply with border controls managed by state agencies, and operate within fiscal, environmental, safety, and competition regulations set by governments.

removed_items: The 2025 LPI 2.0 cover three logistics modes—maritime, aviation, and postal—capturing over 80 percent of global goods trade by value.
The digitization of global supply chains means that shipments are now tracked globally in real time.
Though digitization has reached all transport modes and most logistics services, tracking data are available in a globally uniform format only for maritime, aviation, and postal logistics.
Note: About 46 percent of global goods trade by value is moved in maritime containers (Notteboom, Pallis, and Rodrigue 2022), and 33 percent is moved by air (IATA 2025).

Note: The LPI 2.0 do not cover road and rail logistics because no global source of data on those movements exists, but they cover container tracking on transport corridors, including some road transport (since the container tracking indicators indicate the quality of inland logistics services, including to LLDCs).
While the first-best option would be end-to-end coverage of all shipments through all modes, the current reporting is the best available given the existing data.
Future refinements of the LPI 2.0 could include data for other logistics modes.

Parcel and express shipments are primarily business-to-business (B2B) transactions and are thus comparable to maritime container and air cargo shipments, which are purely B2B.

Note: Refers to direct flights.

Note: For a given economy, postal connectivity is the average of two values: the number of unique origin partners from which postal items are received throughout a year and the number of partner economies to which postal items are shipped during the same period.
There are six core indicators in the LPI 2.0, one connectivity indicator and one time indicator for each of the three logistics modes covered (maritime, air, and postal) (table 1.1).

removed_items: Container export dwell time reflects several constraints that differ from those associated with import dwell time.

To capture these challenges, the LPI 2.0 include four indicators specific to LLDCs: dwell time at port of arrival for a container destined for an LLDC, corridor lead time from port exit to destination, dwell time at destination (clearance facility in the LLDC), and reference dwell time at port of arrival.

It is a benchmark for dwell time at port of arrival for a container destined for an LLDC.
Corridor lead time provides information on road or rail corridor performance.
Note: It does not provide information on the performance of multimodal transfers en route, which are included in dwell time instead of lead time.

B2C and B2B shipments typically face different customs procedures.
Historically, B2C shipments (unlike B2B) benefited from de minimis exemptions.
But in recent years a growing number of economies have reconsidered these exemptions and increased scrutiny of B2C shipments, which has been associated with longer delays.
Note: The LPI 2.0 differentiate between B2C and B2B flows because they are associated with different mail types.
Parcels and express mail are attributed to B2B operations, whereas standard letter-post mail is attributed to B2C operations.
Letter-post is used for the majority of e-commerce shipments.

International e-commerce is interconnected with postal services: Universal Postal Union members are responsible for handling about two-thirds of letter-parcel (up to 2 kilograms) deliveries across borders.

Universal Postal Union members also manage international express shipments, which account for 5–10 percent of international e-commerce volume, with the rest delivered by commercial operators (Beretzky et al. 2022).
Note: The de minimis rule for imports allows low-value shipments to avoid tariffs and customs processing.
For imports into the United States, this rule began being phased out in August 2025.

Connecting to Compete 2025 introduces the Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0), a fundamental redesign of the World Bank’s former survey-based Logistics Performance Index toward a system grounded in shipment-level data.

Drawing on large-scale tracking data from maritime, aviation, and postal operators—together accounting for over 80 percent of global goods trade—the LPI 2.0 provide standardized and comparable measures of supply chain connectivity, speed, and reliability across economies and over time.

The framework comprises 21 indicators, including 6 core indicators capturing direct connectivity and import time performance in each mode and 15 supplementary indicators that shed light on maritime competition, transshipment dependence, corridor performance for landlocked developing countries, and postal logistics for e-commerce.

Data for 2023–24 reveal large variations in connectivity across regions, substantial time penalties associated with transshipment and border procedures, and high unpredictability concentrated at ports, transshipment hubs, and inland checkpoints—particularly for imports and for landlocked countries.

By shifting the focus from perceptions to observed outcomes, the LPI 2.0 significantly enhance diagnostic precision and policy relevance, enabling governments to better prioritize reforms with the highest potential impact on supply chain connectivity, speed, reliability, and resilience.

Logistics underpins the movement of goods and the operation of supply chains within and across borders.
Efficient logistics reduces trade costs, connects firms to markets, and supports development, greatly increasing the volume and value of trade.
Recent disruptions have underscored that resilient, well-functioning global logistics networks are essential for growth and welfare.

They help countries withstand shocks, such as natural disasters, conflict, and technical failures, by ensuring reliable access to strategic goods that are too costly or impossible to produce domestically.
The Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0) represent a major methodological shift toward shipment-level, real-world evidence.

There are large connectivity gaps across and within regions.

On average, the Europe and Central Asia region and the North America region tend to exhibit the strongest connectivity, depending on the logistics mode, while Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean lag behind.

Although logistics services are provided mainly by private operators, public policy is fundamental to the performance of global supply and value chains.
The LPI 2.0 enable governments to prioritize interventions with the highest potential impact on supply chain speed, reliability, and resilience, tailored to country circumstances.
A series of disruptions of global logistics networks in recent years has underlined how well-functioning logistics networks are essential to production and welfare worldwide.

Resilient logistics networks strengthen economies’ capacity to withstand natural disasters, conflict, technical failures, or other shocks by securing reliable access to strategic goods (such as pharmaceuticals, food, energy, and technologies) that are prohibitively costly to produce domestically or cannot be produced at all.
Note: The World Bank’s Global Supply Chain Stress Index measures the magnitude of container shipping disruptions affecting global supply chains.

Drawing on observations of logistics activity collected throughout the year, the LPI 2.0 offer a more comprehensive view of structural performance and reduce the influence of temporary shocks or short-lived events on the results.
Three core components define logistics performance: time, reliability, and cost.
The LPI 2.0 measure time and reliability and capture features of logistics services that influence costs.
They do so through indicators in two areas: connectivity and time.
Connectivity refers to the number of markets an economy can directly trade with without having to go through intermediaries and the number and types of services available.
Time refers to the time that logistics processes take and their dispersion, which captures the reliability of the logistics processes.
Both connectivity and time are measured for different logistics modes.

Cost is not directly measured by the LPI 2.0; however, two connectivity indicators highlight competition within the maritime sector, higher degrees of which tend to be associated with lower logistics costs.

Three other maritime indicators gauge how economies could be affected by their dependence on third-country shipping hubs.
These indicators are maritime lead time to import from port of arrival to the destination economy, time spent in transshipment, and number of transshipments for import containers.

Executive summary
Logistics underpins the movement of goods
and the operation of supply chains within and
across borders. Efficient logistics reduces trade
costs, connects firms to markets, and supports
development, greatly increasing the volume and
value of trade. Recent disruptions have under­
scored that resilient, well-­functioning global
logistics networks are essential for growth and
welfare. They help countries withstand shocks,
such as natural disasters, conflict, and technical
failures, by ensuring reliable access to strategic
goods that are too costly or impossible to pro­
duce domestically.
The Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0
(LPI 2.0) represent a major methodological
shift toward shipment-­level, real-­world evidence.
Drawing on large volumes of tracking data
from maritime, aviation, and postal operators­
—­modes that jointly account for more than
80 percent of the global goods trade­—­the LPI
2.0 provide standardized indicators of logistics
performance across economies and time. Unlike
the original Logistics Performance Index (LPI),
which was based on surveys of logistics profes­
sionals, the LPI 2.0 measure the speed, reliabil­
ity, and connectivity of supply chains based on
observed shipment data.1
The LPI 2.0’s 21 indicators provide deep in­
sight into the functioning of logistics networks.
Six core indicators (one connectivity indicator
and one time indicator for maritime, air, and
postal logistics) and 15 supplementary (connec­
tivity and time) indicators provide insights into
maritime competition, transshipment burdens,
corridor performance for landlocked developing
countries (LLDCs), and postal logistics for e-­
commerce. Core connectivity indicators capture
the number of countries that can be reached di­
rectly via maritime, air cargo, or postal services,
while core time indicators measure import
dwell times and delivery times­—­key proxies for
logistics efficiency and reliability.
The shift to LPI 2.0 expands coverage, en­
hances comparability, and deepens diagnostic
power, enabling policymakers to identify bind­
ing constraints with far greater precision. Data
on all 21 indicators are published for 2023 and
2024 at https://lpi.worldbank.org, with op­
tions for comparisons across economies and
over time.
Five main findings stand out from the ana­
lysis of the LPI 2.0:
•	•	 There are large connectivity gaps across
and within regions. On average, the Eu­
rope and Central Asia region and the North
America region tend to exhibit the strongest
connectivity, depending on the logistics
mode, while Sub-­Saharan Africa and Latin
America and the Caribbean lag behind.
These patterns reflect income, geography,
and market accessibility. Within regions,
some developing economies, such as Ma­
laysia, Morocco, and Sri Lanka, showcase
stronger performance due to their emer­
gence as regional hubs.
•	•	 Direct connections matter. Roughly half
of containers worldwide require at least one
transshipment. Each transshipment adds
about 18 days to maritime lead times, cre­
ating structural disadvantages for small, re­
mote economies.
•	•	 Several low- and middle-­income econo­
mies clear imported containers within a
few days, which is comparable to high-­
income economies, while others experi­
ence import dwell times exceeding 10
days. Longer dwell times are due to weak
customs automation, inefficient risk man­
agement, and cumbersome inspection and
clearance processes. Aviation dwell times are

air cargo typically involves smaller volumes,

•	•	 LLDCs face some of the longest and most
unpredictable import times globally,
with most delays stemming from idling
at ports, border controls, and inland
checkpoints. LLDCs must transit coastal
countries, often crossing multiple borders
and facing complex transit procedures. Cor­
ridor lead times and dwell times at the port
of arrival dominate total import time, un­
derscoring the importance of regional coor­

and streamlined border procedures to im­

•	•	 Delays are most unpredictable when

rupts production planning, increases inven­

just-­in-­time and perishable goods markets.
Digital visibility systems, such as those im­
plemented in India and the United States,
demonstrate how the value of real-­time
tracking can mitigate these risks.
Although logistics services are provided
mainly by private operators, public policy is
fundamental to the performance of global sup­
ply and value chains. The LPI 2.0 enable gov­

highest potential impact on supply chain speed,
reliability, and resilience, tailored to country
circumstances. Policy interventions should be
implemented in a targeted, coherent manner
across three strategic areas:
•	•	 Enhancing connectivity. Open transport
and logistics markets to competition, invest
in multimodal corridors and logistics clus­
ters, and use regional integration and shared
connectivity solutions so smaller or remote
economies can benefit from economies of
scale.
Reducing time and variability. Modernize
border management through digitalization
and risk-­based controls (trade facilitation),
improve port and airport performance,
and strengthen traceability to make supply
chains faster and more predictable.
•	•	 Strengthening institutions and regula­
tion. Build a robust governance framework
with transparent public–private partner­
ships, competitive logistics markets, and
coordinated policies across ministries, de­
partments, and agencies to sustain and scale
logistics reforms.

Why is logistics important for trade
and development?
Logistics consists of a set of activities (freight
transportation, warehousing, brokerage) that
move goods and establish supply chains across
and within borders. Logistics performance
captures the efficiency of supply chain connec­
tions, measured in time, cost, and reliability.
Since 2007 the Logistics Performance Index
(LPI) initiative has emphasized the importance
of efficient supply chains in connecting firms to
markets, reducing trade costs, and supporting
development.2 Logistics performance supports
economic development by enabling trade within
and across borders.3
Economics literature, often using the
survey-­based LPI, has established that logistics
performance positively and significantly im­
pacts the volume and value of bilateral trade,
in particular exports.4 Logistics influences the
time required for a product to reach its market.
On average, an increase in inland transit time
of one day reduces exports by 7 percent.5 For
manufactured goods exports the likelihood of
a country exporting to the United States de­
creases by 1.5 percent for each additional day of
shipping time.6
Logistics inefficiencies hamper economies’
competitiveness because logistics affect manu­
facturing firms’ production costs.7 Improved
logistics performance reduces production costs
and is linked to stronger participation in global
value chains.8 This is achieved not just through
lower direct logistics costs (transport, storage,
and administrative costs) but also by reducing
the need for inventory and working capital.9
A series of disruptions of global logistics
networks in recent years has underlined how
well-­functioning logistics networks are essen­
tial to production and welfare worldwide.10
Resilient logistics networks strengthen econo­
mies’ capacity to withstand natural disasters,
conflict, technical failures, or other shocks by
securing reliable access to strategic goods (such
as pharmaceuticals, food, energy, and technolo­
gies) that are prohibitively costly to produce do­
mestically or cannot be produced at all.
Conceptual framework of the LPI 2.0
and evolution from the original LPI
Until 2023 the LPI was based on a survey in
which logistics professionals rated, on a 1–5
scale, the ease of establishing supply chains with
economies they traded with. When the LPI was
conceived in the mid-­2000s, perception-­based
data were the only option. However, survey-­
based indicators have limitations, including per­
ception bias and large year-­on-­year fluctuations.
The Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0
(LPI 2.0) move away from perceptions and rely
instead on objective measures derived from large
volumes of shipment-­level tracking data made
available to the World Bank on a confiden­
tial basis by global industry and international
tracking initiatives. These data provide granu­
lar measures of the speed and connectivity of
international supply chains worldwide. Draw­
ing on observations of logistics activity collected
throughout the year, the LPI 2.0 offer a more
comprehensive view of structural performance
and reduce the influence of temporary shocks
or short-­lived events on the results.
Three core components define logistics per­
formance: time, reliability, and cost. The LPI 2.0
measure time and reliability and capture features
of logistics services that influence costs. They do
so through indicators in two areas: connectiv­
ity and time. Connectivity refers to the number
of markets an economy can directly trade with
without having to go through intermediaries

and the number and types of services available.
Time refers to the time that logistics processes
take and their dispersion, which captures the re­
liability of the logistics processes. Both connec­
tivity and time are measured for different logis­
tics modes. Cost is not directly measured by the
LPI 2.0; however, two connectivity indicators
highlight competition within the maritime sec­
tor, higher degrees of which tend to be associated
with lower logistics costs.11
The 2025 LPI 2.0 cover three logistics
modes—maritime, aviation, and postal—cap­
turing over 80 percent of global goods trade by
value.12 The digitization of global supply chains
means that shipments are now tracked globally
in real time. Though digitization has reached
all transport modes and most logistics services,
tracking data are available in a globally uniform
format only for maritime, aviation, and postal
logistics.13
The new indicators
The indicators that make up the LPI 2.0 mea­
sure the connectivity and time of international
trade supply chains, including the time ship­
ments spend at key nodes such as seaports and
airports. The LPI 2.0 consist of 21 indicators,
each reported at the economy level and with dif­
ferent statistical measures.14
Core indicators
There are six core indicators in the LPI 2.0, one
connectivity indicator and one time indicator
for each of the three logistics modes covered
(maritime, air, and postal) (table 1.1). The core
maritime connectivity indicator is the number
of unique economies that are reachable from
and that can reach a given economy through
direct maritime services operated by liner ship­
ping companies on a predefined rotation.15
The core aviation connectivity indicator is the
average number of economies that are reach­
able from and that can reach a given economy
through direct cargo-­carrying air transport
services.16 The core postal connectivity indica­
tor is the average number of economies with
inbound and outbound postal connections for
parcel and express shipments with a given econ­
omy.17 Parcel and express shipments are primar­
ily business-­to-­business (B2B) transactions and
are thus comparable to maritime container and
air cargo shipments, which are purely B2B.
Connectivity is positively associated with
logistics performance across all modes. More
connected economies can directly reach a larger
number of trade partners and tend to face lower
trade costs. Higher connectivity increases
competition among logistics service provid­
ers and encourages investment in trade-­related
infrastructure, such as ports and information
technology systems. It is also associated with a
stronger presence of global logistics operators,
which facilitates the diffusion of best practices
and can generate positive spillovers for domestic
logistics services. Connectivity is also critical for
resilience. Economies that rely on only one or a
few international partners are more vulnerable
to disruptions when those links break down,

The core time indicators measure the time
it takes to import cargo. The core maritime and

generally more complex and time-­consuming

Import dwell and delivery times capture
the efficiency of several components of trade
logistics, including customs clearance and
border management; seaport and airport oper­
ations (such as terminal operations, cargo han­
dling, and yard management); cargo removal
practices;18 land transport services (including
the availability of trucks or other equipment for
onward transport); and the quality of transport
and logistics infrastructure.
Supplementary indicators
While the six core indicators provide a solid
overview of an economy’s logistics performance,
the LPI 2.0 provide additional connectivity and
time indicators for maritime and postal logistics
to measure performance more precisely (table
1.2). Two supplementary maritime connectiv­
ity indicators—the number of direct container
liner shipping services and alliances servicing
the ports in an economy—highlight competi­
tion within the sector,19 higher degrees of which
tend to be associated with better performance

time indicators gauge how economies could be
affected by their dependence on third-­country
shipping hubs. These indicators are maritime
lead time to import from port of arrival to the
destination economy, time spent in transship­
ment, and number of transshipments for import
containers. Two indicators that are derived from
empty container movements—export supply
chain initiation and import supply chain termi­
nation—reflect logistics efficiency among ship­
pers, consignees, and trucking companies.
Two supplementary maritime time indica­
tors capture additional aspects of performance
at ports. Turnaround time (twenty-­foot equiva­
lent unit weighted and unweighted) reflects in­
vestment in port capacity and handling equip­
ment, as well as the performance of terminal
operations. Container export dwell time re­
flects several constraints that differ from those
associated with import dwell time. Controls
applied to export shipments are typically mild
compared with those applied to imports, even in
economies with long import delays. Formalities
such as obtaining certificates of origin, which
are processed upstream, are not automated in
many economies and may delay containers.
Furthermore, export dwell time includes buffer
time, voluntary or mandated by the shipping
lines (such as 48 hours in advance of ship de­
parture). Factors such as export-­import imbal­
ances, distance to port, and frequency of ship­
ping connections may influence private sector
strategy and buffer time.
Traders in LLDCs face the challenge that
their shipments usually travel long distances by
land and cross land borders. To capture these
challenges, the LPI 2.0 include four indicators
specific to LLDCs: dwell time at port of arrival
for a container destined for an LLDC, corridor
lead time from port exit to destination, dwell
time at destination (clearance facility in the
LLDC), and reference dwell time at port of ar­
rival. A comprehensive measure of container im­
port time for LLDCs is the sum of the first three
indicators. The fourth indicator measures import
dwell time for containers destined for the coastal
economy that is typically used as the transit econ­
omy for an LLDC. It is a benchmark for dwell
time at port of arrival for a container destined for
an LLDC. Corridor lead time provides informa­
tion on road or rail corridor performance.21
The supplementary postal logistics indica­
tors are similar to the core indicators but focus
on business-­to-­consumer (B2C) shipments,
which are mostly e-­commerce orders.22 B2C
and B2B shipments typically face different cus­
toms procedures. Historically, B2C shipments
(unlike B2B) benefited from de minimis exemp­
tions.23 But in recent years a growing number of
economies have reconsidered these exemptions
and increased scrutiny of B2C shipments, which
has been associated with longer delays.
Data
Since the launch of the LPI in 2007, the rapid
digitization of global supply chains has trans­
formed the availability and granularity of logis­
tics data. The 2025 LPI 2.0 leverage this shift
by moving beyond perception-­based surveys and
drawing on large-­scale shipment-­level tracking
data obtained under information-­sharing agree­
ments with global operators.24 The World Bank
collaborated with international carriers and
data providers to assemble a multimodal data­
set covering maritime shipping, air cargo, and
postal services. This approach enables more
objective, timely, and comparable indicators
across economies.
The LPI 2.0 expand coverage relative to ear­
lier editions, including many LLDCs and small
island states that were previously excluded due
to data gaps. Coverage remains limited for a
small number of economies affected by embar­
goes or severe conflict, where global logistics
operators have little or no presence. The dataset
reflects actual logistics performance along in­
ternational supply chains rather than national
averages inferred from surveys.
Maritime indicators draw on several com­
plementary sources. Container shipping con­
nectivity is derived from MDS Transmodal’s
Containership Databank, which tracks con­
tainer vessels and provides detailed information
on service frequency and port rotations. Con­
tainer dwell times, lead times, and supply chain
initiation and termination indicators are cal­
culated using shipment-­level data from a major

Aviation and postal indicators complement

Together, these datasets form the empirical
backbone of the LPI 2.0, enabling a more gran­

performance across economies and modes.

This chapter presents high-­level findings from
the Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI
2.0) with a focus on systematic patterns across
regions and income groups. Data on all 21
indicators for 2023 and 2024 are published
at https://lpi.worldbank.org, with options for
comparisons across economies and over time.
Connectivity
On average, the Europe and Central Asia region
and the North America region tend to have the
highest connectivity across logistics modes,
while the Latin America and the Caribbean
region and the Sub-­Saharan Africa region tend
to have the lowest, depending on the mode con­
sidered (figure 2.1, panels a, b, c), although some
developing economies perform strongly. This
pattern mirrors broader income and geographic
differences: high-­income economies are gen­
erally more connected than low- and middle-­
income economies (figure 2.1, panels d, e, f). The
connectivity indicators also reflect an economy’s
position in the global shipping network and its
proximity to centers of economic activity.
Developing economies that have emerged as
regional or global shipping hubs, such as Malay­
sia, Morocco, and Sri Lanka, have much higher
connectivity than their neighbors with the same
accessibility. For the same level of market acces­
sibility, larger economies have more connections­
—­for instance, Australia and New Zealand,
which are among the economies with the low­
est accessibility, have the highest connectivity at
that level of accessibility (figure 2.2).
Connectivity increased during 2023–24
across most regions. Between 2023 and 2024
the number of direct liner shipping, aviation,
and postal services connections increased across
most income groups and regions, though some
economies in South Asia and in the Middle East
and North Africa showed a small decline (see
figure 2.1). These declines in maritime connec­
tivity occurred largely because of the Red Sea
crisis.
The existence of direct maritime connec­
tions matters because it removes significant
delays associated with transshipments. Though
about half of containers travel directly to their
destination, the rest may be transshipped mul­
tiple times­—­up to eight in some cases (figure
2.3, panel a). Small island states are the most
affected, with several averaging more than two
transshipments in 2024: São Tomé and Príncipe
(2.6), Anguilla (2.4), the Comoros (2.4), and St.
Kitts and Nevis (2.2). Each transshipment adds
to maritime lead times­—­roughly 18 extra days
per transfer­—­underscoring the heavy burden
of hub dependence for these economies (figure
2.3, panel b). But the hub and spoke structure
of modern long-­distance supply chains, where
smaller freight loads are consolidated into larger
ones at hubs using high-­capacity equipment, has
proven cost-­effective for carriers while providing
small and peripheral economies with access to
global routes.
Time
Several low- and middle-­income economies have
moderate container import dwell times, similar
to those in high-­income economies, but many
have exceptionally long ones (more than two
weeks). Most of the economies with excessive
dwell time are in Sub-­Saharan Africa and in the
Middle East and North Africa. Aviation import
dwell time is typically only half of container
import dwell time or less (figure 2.4). This dif­
ference reflects the smaller volume, smaller size,
and higher value of air cargo compared with

The economies with the shortest dwell times are

Long container import dwell times often re­

times are more common in Latin America and
the Caribbean and in Sub-­Saharan Africa.

matter: The postal indicator includes both the
time spent at the postal bureau of entry and the
time until delivery, which can be prolonged when
domestic postal networks are not optimized, par­
ticularly in geographically large economies. Sec­
ond, customs clearance practices play a key role.
In some economies, including several in Latin
America and the Caribbean, inbound shipment
information is not electronically linked to cus­
toms systems, so clearance relies on paper docu­
mentation for each shipment, increasing delays.
The special situation of landlocked
developing countries
Landlocked developing countries (LLDCs) are
among the most logistically constrained coun­
tries because their cargo needs to transit through
coastal countries, crossing more than one bor­
der. As a result, the time to import a container
is exceptionally long and uneven for LLDCs.
Among the three components of time to import
for LLDCs, corridor lead time and dwell time
at port of arrival in coastal country tend to be
the largest, followed by dwell time at destination
(figure 2.5). In addition, dwell time at the port
of arrival is longer for goods in transit than for
goods destined for coastal countries.28
The long import times are not explained by
corridor distance but by the considerable time
cargo spends idling at ports, at borders, and in
checkpoints along transit corridors en route to
the LLDCs—reinforcing the importance of
pursuing corridor reforms. These reforms in­
clude tackling border crossing delays, improving
exchange of information on transit vehicles and
goods across borders, and adopting better transit
procedures and guarantee mechanisms. Among
the biggest technical challenges is cross-­border
interoperability of financial guarantees or bonds
covering the customs value of goods in transit.
The best practice systems are the Transports In­
ternationaux Routiers system (managed by the
International Road Union and used in Central
Asia and the Balkans) and the Common Transit
procedure (applicable to European Union and
European Free Trade Association countries). Ex­
cept for the Secretary of Economic Integration
of Central America transit system, these systems
have not been fully adopted by other regions.

Chapter 2  What the LPI 2.0 reveals about logistics performance
in ports, border controls, and inland check­
points. The LPI 2.0 assess supply chain reli­
ability at the economy level through the inter­
quartile range of dwell, delivery, and lead times
(figure 2.6).29 Dispersion increases with median
dwell times and is, on average, 36 percent higher
for imports than for exports (figure 2.7). Dis­
persion is even higher for aviation supply chains.
In well-­functioning ports with seamless
clearance systems, processing an unloaded con­
tainer starts immediately. In Le Havre (France)
10 percent of containers leave the port in 1 day
or less, 50 percent do so in 3.8 days or less, and
only 25 percent take more than 5.9 days (figure
2.8). By contrast, in many ports only a few con­
tainers are cleared during the first few days after
arrival. In Apapa (Nigeria) only 0.2 percent of
containers leave the port in 1 day or less, 50 per­
cent do so in 13.4 days or less, and 25 percent
take more than 22.1 days, and in Algiers (Alge­
ria), only 0.1 percent leave the port in 1 day or
less, 50 percent do so in 17.6 days, and 25 per­
cent take more than 26.3 days.

port clearance processes and port operations,

In some low- and middle-­income economies

upper-­middle- and high-­income economies the
average weighted turnaround time is less than
two days, compared with two to six days in sev­
eral low- and lower-­middle-­income economies.
These differences point to substantial scope
for improving container port performance in
low- and lower-­middle-­income economies.31

turnaround time typically being much shorter
than container import dwell time (figure 2.9,
panel b). Though dwell time is influenced by
infrastructure, it captures primarily the perfor­
mance of customs and other border procedures
and therefore depends largely on trade facilita­
tion policies.
Strong B2B and business-­to-­consumer
(B2C) postal logistics performance is critical
for e-commerce and SME participation. Al­
though standard postal services experienced
considerable market erosion in 2023 and 2024,
they continue to play a substantial role in the
last-­mile delivery of cross-­border e-­commerce
shipments (B2C), with close to 40  percent
of these items being delivered by traditional
postal services in 2024.32 Poor postal logistics
performance tends to constrain small and me­
dium enterprises (SMEs) from participating in
e-­commerce, with B2C SMEs usually finding it
harder to scale up than B2B SMEs because B2C
business entails a higher intensity of shipping.33
Furthermore, B2C postal delivery times tend
to be longer than B2B delivery times, primar­
ily in lower-­middle-­income economies, pointing
to inconsistencies in postal logistics that penal­
ize firms engaged in B2C e-­commerce in these
economies (figure 2.10).

CHAPTER
3 From indicators to policy interventions
Logistics services—such as freight transporta­
tion, warehousing, and brokerage—are deliv­
ered primarily by private firms. But their effi­
ciency and the overall performance of supply
chains are fundamentally shaped by public
policy. Logistics operations depend on publicly
funded infrastructure, must comply with border
controls managed by state agencies, and operate
within fiscal, environmental, safety, and compe­
tition regulations set by governments.
A strategic framework for logistics
performance
Policy interventions to improve logistics per­
formance, as measured by the LPI 2.0, should
be implemented in a targeted, coherent manner
across three strategic areas:
•	•	 Enhancing connectivity through strategic
investment and liberalization.
Reducing time and variability through trade
facilitation and infrastructure.
•	•	 Strengthening the institutional and regula­
tory environment for logistics.
Together with reforms to reduce logistics
costs—which are not directly measured by the
LPI 2.0—these areas provide a practical policy
agenda for governments seeking to improve lo­
gistics performance.
Area 1: Enhancing connectivity through
strategic investment and liberalization
A country’s connectivity to global production
and distribution networks is determined by its
physical geography, the quality and reach of its
transport infrastructure, and the network strate­
gies of international operators. While geography
is fixed, public policy can greatly influence how
well a country is connected to global markets.
Governments can act on three main fronts.
1.1  Liberalizing markets for transport and
logistics services. Policies that open markets
to competition and foreign participation can
encourage international operators to expand
their networks and increase the number of part­
ner economies served. Examples include:
•	•	 Liberalizing maritime services and port op­
erations to attract global shipping lines and
terminal operators.
•	•	 Adopting “Open Skies” agreements in avia­
tion to allow more carriers, routes, and fre­
quencies.
•	•	 Removing restrictive regulations that limit
entry or capacity in key logistics services
(e.g., freight forwarding, express delivery).
These measures can increase service fre­
quency, reduce costs, and improve the reliability
of international connections.
1.2  Developing hubs, corridors, and logis­
tics clusters. Governments can use infrastruc­
ture planning and spatial policies to position
their economies as attractive nodes in regional
and global networks. This involves:
•	•	 Investing in and upgrading gateway ports,
airports, and dry ports that can serve as re­
gional hubs.
•	•	 Developing multimodal transport corridors
that connect these gateways to major pro­
duction and consumption centers.
•	•	 Promoting logistics and industrial clusters
around key hubs through zoning, serviced
land, and streamlined permitting.
These policies can help transform a coun­
try’s connectivity and establish it as a regional
logistics and manufacturing hub.
1.3  Pursuing regional integration and
shared connectivity solutions. For small,
landlocked, or remote economies, national

policies alone may not be sufficient to achieve
scale. Regional cooperation becomes essential.
Key governments include:
•	•	 Harmonizing regulations and technical
standards with partner economies to facili­
tate cross-border transport and logistics.
•	•	 Developing regional transit regimes and
corridor management institutions to ensure
seamless movement of goods.
•	•	 Coordinating investment in regional gate­
ways and corridors so that smaller econo­
mies can “piggyback” on the trade flows
of larger neighbors and global distribution
centers.
By pursuing these policies, governments
can systematically improve their connectivity
performance, making their economies more
attractive for trade and participation in global
value chains.
Area 2: Reducing time and variability
through trade facilitation and
infrastructure
Time-related indicators—such as dwell time
in ports and airports, ship turnaround time,
and postal delivery time—are more respon­
sive to policy than connectivity indicators
are. Reducing delays and variability is criti­
cal for modern supply chains, especially those
integrated into just-in-time production and
e-commerce.
Governments can influence time and reli­
ability through three main sets of policies.
2.1  Modernizing border management and
trade facilitation. Border procedures are often
a major source of delays and uncertainty. Key
reforms include:
•	•	 Implementing risk-based management sys­
tems to focus inspections on high-risk con­
signments and expedite low-risk trade.
•	•	 Digitizing customs and border processes,
including electronic submission of docu­
ments, prearrival processing, and electronic
payment of duties and fees.
•	•	 Establishing coordinated border manage­
ment, where customs and other border agen­
cies (e.g., health, agriculture, security) align
procedures and share information.
•	•	 For landlocked countries, designing and
implementing efficient transit regimes, in­
cluding transit guarantees, bonded trans­
port, and streamlined procedures at border
crossings.
These measures can greatly reduce import
and export dwell times and improve the predict­
ability of clearance processes.
2.2  Improving gateway efficiency and ter­
minal operations. Even when border proce­
dures are efficient, poor performance at ports,
airports, and inland terminals can create bottle­
necks. Government actions can include:
•	•	 Investing in infrastructure to address ca­
pacity constraints, such as berth extensions,
yard expansion, and improved access roads
and rail links.
•	•	 Promoting operational improvements, in­
cluding port community systems, electronic
appointment systems for truck arrivals, per­
formance-based contracts with terminal op­
erators, and efficient pricing of port storage.
•	•	 Using public–private partnerships (PPPs) to
bring in private expertise and capital for ter­
minal management, with clear performance
targets for productivity and service quality.
These policies directly affect ship turn­
around time, container dwell time, and the reli­
ability of gateway operations.
2.3  Enhancing supply chain traceability and
predictability. For firms participating in global
value chains, predictability is often as important
as speed. Governments can support more pre­
dictable logistics by:
•	•	 Addressing upstream causes of delays, such
as complex banking procedures for foreign
exchange, documentation requirements, or
licensing processes that hold up shipments
before they reach customs.
•	•	 Encouraging the use of digital tracking and
tracing systems, including integration of
customs, port, and logistics operator (in­
cluding postal services) data.
•	•	 Supporting the development of express lo­
gistics and time-definite delivery services,
which rely on streamlined customs proce­
dures and integrated handling at gateways.

By focusing on both the direct and indirect
sources of delay, governments can save time, re­
duce variability, and improve the reliability of
supply chains.
Area 3: Strengthening the institutional
and regulatory environment for logistics
Physical investments and trade facilitation
reforms are most effective when supported by
a sound institutional and regulatory environ­
ment. This area focuses on how governments
organize, regulate, and coordinate the logistics
sector. Governments can do so in three key pol­
icy areas.
3.1  Leveraging public–private partner­
ships and improving sector governance.
PPPs, when well designed and embedded in a
clear policy framework, can be powerful tools
to improve logistics performance. Governments
should consider:
•	•	 Using PPPs for port, airport, and inland
terminal operations where private opera­
tors can bring management expertise, tech­
nology, and investment.
•	•	 Defining transparent concession frame­
works with measurable performance indi­
cators (e.g., crane productivity, truck turn­
around time, dwell time) and mechanisms
for monitoring and enforcement.
Ensuring that PPPs are aligned with broader
logistics and trade strategies rather than ne­
gotiated as isolated deals.
3.2  Strengthening competition, market
structure, and supporting domestic logistics
development. A competitive and professional
logistics services market is essential for efficient
supply chains. Policy priorities include:
•	•	 Removing unnecessary barriers to entry
and anticompetitive regulations in truck­
ing, freight forwarding, warehousing, and
express delivery.
•	•	 Modernizing trucking regulations (e.g., axle
load limits, vehicle standards, licensing) to
balance safety and environmental objectives
with efficiency.
Opening markets to private and foreign pro­
viders where appropriate, while ensuring a
level playing field and effective competition
oversight.
•	•	 Supporting the development of higher
value-added logistics services (e.g., third-
party logistics, contract logistics, cold chain)
through clear regulations and investment-
friendly policies.
These measures help improve domestic lo­
gistics performance and enable firms to access
more sophisticated services, which in turn sup­
ports better connectivity and shorter delivery
times.
3.3  Enhancing policy consistency, coordi­
nation, and implementation capacity. Con­
nectivity and logistics performance improve
gradually as operators adjust their networks and
investment. Governments therefore need:
•	•	 Stable, predictable policy frameworks that
give investors confidence to commit capital
to infrastructure and logistics services.
Institutional mechanisms—such as national
logistics councils or trade facilitation com­
mittees—to coordinate across ministries
(transport, trade, finance, customs, indus­
try) and with the private sector.
•	•	 Clear national logistics or trade facilitation
strategies with measurable targets linked to
key performance indicators, such as those in
the LPI 2.0, and systems to monitor prog­
ress and adjust policies as needed.
•	•	 Strengthened implementation capacity in
customs, port authorities, transport agen­
cies, and other relevant institutions, includ­
ing training, change management, and ad­
equate resourcing.
A coherent institutional and regulatory en­
vironment ensures that reforms under the first
two areas are sustained and that their benefits
are fully realized.
Using the LPI 2.0 to prioritize and
tailor reforms
Logistics reform is not a one-size-fits-all
endeavor. Economies differ in geography, eco­
nomic structure, institutional capacity, and
political economy. The LPI 2.0 provides a struc­
tured way to diagnose performance gaps in

connectivity and time and to link those gaps to
specific policy levers.
By organizing interventions under three
areas—­enhancing connectivity, reducing time
and variability, and strengthening institutions
and regulations—governments can:
•	•	 Identify the root causes of logistics frictions.
•	•	 Prioritize the reforms with the highest ex­
pected impact on supply chain performance
and trade outcomes.
•	•	 Sequence interventions in a way that re­
flects their capacity and socio-political
context.
Ultimately, the value of the LPI 2.0 lies not
only in measuring logistics performance but
also in guiding governments toward concrete,
evidence-based policy actions that improve
connectivity, reduce time to trade, and sup­
port integration into regional and global value
chains.

What are the Logistics Performance Indicators (LPI 2.0)?
The LPI 2.0 is an interactive benchmarking tool created to help countries identify the
challenges and opportunities they face in their performance on trade logistics and
discover what they can do to improve their performance. Connecting to Compete
2025 introduces the LPI 2.0, a fundamental redesign of the World Bank’s former
Logistics Performance Index from a survey-based index toward a system grounded
in shipment-level data. Drawing on large-scale tracking data from maritime, aviation,
and postal operators—together accounting for over 80 percent of global goods
trade—the LPI 2.0 provide standardized and comparable measures of supply chain
speed, reliability, and connectivity across economies and over time. The framework
comprises 21 indicators, including 6 core indicators capturing direct connectivity
and import time performance in each mode and 15 supplementary indicators that
shed light on maritime competition, transshipment dependence, postal logistics for
e-commerce, and corridor performance for landlocked developing countries.
This is the eighth edition of Connecting to Compete, a report
summarizing the ﬁndings from the new dataset for the Logistics
Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0). The 2025 LPI 2.0 draw on
supply chain tracking data from the movers of international trade.
This information is relevant for policymakers and decisionmakers
in the private sector seeking to identify reform priorities for trade
and logistics infrastructure. Data for 2023–24 reveal large
variations in connectivity across regions, substantial time penalties
associated with transshipment and border procedures, and high
unpredictability concentrated at ports, transshipment hubs, and
inland checkpoints—particularly for imports and for landlocked
countries. By shifting the focus from perceptions to observed
outcomes, the LPI 2.0 signiﬁcantly enhance diagnostic precision and
policy relevance, enabling governments to better prioritize reforms
with the highest potential impact on supply chain connectivity, speed,
reliability, and resilience.
